title: United States v. Gayle — Rohan Ingram foreign predicate conviction
lead: Firearms found in Rohan Ingram’s hotel room led to a federal possession conviction based on an earlier Canadian offense. His appeal asked whether Congress’s reference to conviction in any court extended to foreign tribunals.

actors.name: Rohan Ingram
actors.role: Appellant whose Canadian conviction supplied the disputed firearm predicate

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Prosecutor supporting inclusion of foreign convictions

actors.name: Judge Katzmann
actors.role: Author of the unanimous Second Circuit opinion

proceedings: The district court denied dismissal, and a jury convicted Ingram on three counts. The Second Circuit reversed only the felon-in-possession conviction and remanded for resentencing on the surviving conspiracy counts.
limits: The ruling excluded foreign convictions as a class rather than testing each foreign judicial system. Small v. United States later endorsed a domestic-only reading in a different defendant’s case. This account does not certify current statutory or administrative-deference law.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A Canadian conviction became a federal predicate
sections.cue: Identify the defendant behind the broader case caption.
paragraphs: In 1996, Rohan Ingram was convicted in Canada of using a firearm in commission of an indictable offense under Canadian Criminal Code section 85(1)(a). Although his actual sentence was less than one year, the offense carried a fourteen-year maximum.

On February 16, 2001, authorities arrested Ingram at a hotel in Plattsburgh, New York, suspecting illegal entry from Canada. They found numerous firearms boxed in his room. A superseding indictment charged conspiracy to export defense articles on the United States Munitions List, conspiracy to travel intending illegally to acquire firearms, and firearm possession by someone with a qualifying prior conviction under 18 U.S.C. sections 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2). Gayle and Richardson appeared in the case caption, but Ingram’s Canadian conviction generated this appeal’s interpretive question.

sections.title: The district court read any court broadly
sections.cue: Trace conviction and the limited appellate challenge.
paragraphs: Ingram sought dismissal of the possession count because the earlier conviction came from outside the United States. The Northern District of New York denied his motion, reading any court as unambiguously including foreign tribunals. It also held that the imprisonment threshold referred to the offense’s maximum punishment, not Ingram’s actual sentence; he did not challenge that ruling on appeal.

A jury convicted him on all three counts on October 5, 2001. On January 30, 2002, he received seventy-eight months in prison, three years of supervised release, and a $300 assessment. The court denied his acquittal motion on February 5. The Second Circuit reviewed statutory interpretation anew. A separately filed order affirmed refusal to suppress the firearms; the foreign-predicate opinion did not supply that order’s reasoning.

sections.title: The surrounding statute complicated the broad reading
sections.cue: Explain why the panel found ambiguity.
paragraphs: Section 922(g)(1), part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, bars specified firearm transactions and possession by a person convicted in any court of a crime punishable by more than one year’s imprisonment. The government’s reading had textual force: an unrestricted modifier could reach many kinds of court, earlier decisions had included military courts, and dangerous people convicted abroad could threaten the statute’s protective purpose. The Third, Fourth, and Sixth Circuits included foreign courts. The Tenth Circuit’s contrary Concha decision involved a sentencing enhancement but relied on the same predicate language.

Judge Katzmann, writing for Judges McLaughlin and Leval as well as himself, nevertheless found ambiguity in context. Section 921(a)(20) excluded specified federal or state business-regulation offenses, including antitrust crimes, and certain state misdemeanors. A reading reaching foreign courts would make foreign antitrust convictions disabling when equivalent domestic convictions were excluded. That asymmetry weakened the claim that any necessarily reached every country’s courts.

Statutory references to officials or governmental acts can also carry an implicit domestic domain. A state’s authorization for a police officer to arrest does not necessarily empower foreign police. Court could similarly refer to domestic institutions without an express geographic modifier. These considerations, alongside the plausible argument for foreign violent-crime predicates, established ambiguity rather than resolving the question by text alone.

sections.title: Legislative history supplied the domestic scope
sections.cue: Explain the inference without substituting an unenacted text.
paragraphs: The panel consulted the Senate Judiciary Committee report, which described felony in federal and state terms. The Conference Report adopted the House’s punishment-based formulation instead of the Senate’s felony terminology, but did not reject the domestic limitation or discuss foreign convictions. The panel inferred domestic scope from those authoritative materials surrounding enactment; it did not treat the Senate wording as the final statutory text.

On rehearing, a seventh note answered the government’s claim that earlier firearm prohibitions mattered more than the legislative activity surrounding the 1968 Act. The panel declined to disregard authoritative history accompanying enactment of the ambiguous provision. The added explanation did not alter the judgment.

Foreign predicates also raised unanswered questions about convictions obtained through procedures inconsistent with basic justice or for religious disobedience or criticism of government. Those concerns reinforced the contextual doubt. They did not create a screening system for acceptable foreign convictions. The panel concluded that Congress had not sufficiently expressed an intent to include foreign convictions, without questioning Congress’s constitutional ability to do so.

sources.pinpoint: original ¶¶21–27 & nn.5–6; amended Appendix A n.7

sections.title: The regulation did not control the criminal statute
sections.cue: Distinguish interpretive tools and the exact result.
paragraphs: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms had a regulation expressly including federal, state, and foreign offenses. After supplemental briefing, both parties agreed that its criminal-statute interpretation did not receive Chevron deference, the administrative-law doctrine then associated with agency readings of ambiguous statutes. The agency’s explanation relied on existing court decisions, and neither it nor those decisions addressed the legislative materials the panel found significant. Although the panel discussed Concha’s use of lenity, it resolved this ambiguity through context and legislative history rather than automatically favoring the defendant at the first sign of ambiguity.

The Second Circuit reversed Ingram’s felon-in-possession conviction and remanded for resentencing on the remaining conspiracy convictions. No judge wrote separately. Small v. United States, 544 U.S. 385 (2005), later endorsed a domestic-only interpretation, but arose from another defendant’s Third Circuit case, not Supreme Court review of Ingram’s appeal.
